full_text_en:
Zaozhuang Mining (Group) Co., Ltd., Chaili Coal Mine v.  
Huaxia Bank Co., Ltd., Qingdao Branch, and  
Qingdao Free Trade Zone Huadong International Trade Co., Ltd.  
— Dispute over joint venture contract  

【Ruling Summary】  

For contract clauses that are unclear in their terms and disputed by the parties, various interpretative methods, including the purpose of the contract, may be used to comprehensively ascertain the true intent of the parties when entering into the contract. However, in terms of purposive interpretation, it should not be based solely on the contractual purpose that one party expects to achieve. Instead, interpretation should be based on the common contractual purpose of the parties as ordinarily understood by a rational third party who has no interest in the contract. Moreover, purposive interpretation should not lead to an infringement of the lawful rights and interests of others or conflict with laws and regulations.  

Civil Judgment of the Supreme People's Court  

(2009) Min Ti Zi No. 137  

Applicant for Retrial (Plaintiff at First Instance, Appellee at Second Instance, Original Respondent for Retrial): Zaozhuang Mining (Group) Co., Ltd., Chaili Coal Mine, domiciled at: Xigang Town, Tengzhou City, Shandong Province.  

Responsible Person: Cheng Zhaoxiang, Mine Director of the said mine.  

Agent ad litem: Zhang Huaifu, Director of the Legal Department of the said mine.  

Agent ad litem: Li Cunyang, Lawyer of Beijing Yijia Law Firm.  

Respondent (Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance, Original Applicant for Retrial): Huaxia Bank Co., Ltd., Qingdao Branch, domiciled at: Galaxy Building, No. 29 Shandong Road, Qingdao City, Shandong Province.  

Responsible Person: Guan Wenjie, President of the said branch.  

Agent ad litem: Guo Bin, Lawyer of Shandong Chenggong Law Firm.  

Agent ad litem: Yu Guankui, Lawyer of Shandong Chenggong Law Firm.  

Defendant at First Instance, Appellant at Second Instance: Qingdao Free Trade Zone Huadong International Trade Co., Ltd., domiciled at: Room C/D, 21F, Building 1Z, No. 35 Donghai Road, Qingdao City, Shandong Province.  

Legal Representative: Sun Yan, Chairperson of the said company.  

Agent ad litem: Liu Xueliang, Assistant to the Chairperson of the said company.  

Agent ad litem: Dai Meng, Lawyer of Shandong Quandu Law Firm.  

The applicant for retrial, Zaozhuang Mining (Group) Co., Ltd., Chaili Coal Mine (hereinafter referred to as Chaili Coal Mine), dissatisfied with the civil judgment (2007) Lu Min Zai Zi No. 123 rendered by the Shandong High People's Court on July 13, 2008, in the dispute over a joint venture contract with the respondent Huaxia Bank Co., Ltd., Qingdao Branch (hereinafter referred to as Huaxia Bank) and Qingdao Free Trade Zone Huadong International Trade Co., Ltd. (hereinafter referred to as Huadong Company), filed an application for retrial with this Court. This Court rendered the civil ruling (2008) Min Zai Shen Zi No. 47 on April 7, 2009, ordering a retrial of this case. This Lawful formed a collegial panel to hear the case, and the trial has now been concluded.  

On May 23, 2005, Chaili Coal Mine filed a lawsuit with the Tengzhou City People's Court of Shandong Province, alleging: On March 16, 2004, it entered into the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" with Huadong Company and Huaxia Bank, which stipulated: Chaili Coal Mine and Huadong Company would jointly operate Indonesian timber; Chaili Coal Mine was responsible for providing RMB 10 million in funds, which were to be remitted to Huaxia Bank by March 18, 2004, as requested by Huadong Company, and Huadong Company would handle the application for issuance of letters of credit for international trade; when handling the application for issuance of letters of credit for international trade, a written consent opinion from Wen Zhongcheng, the responsible person of Chaili Coal Mine, was required, and Huaxia Bank, upon seeing Wen Zhongcheng's written consent opinion, would handle the issuance of letters of credit in accordance with the terms jointly applied for by both parties; the profits from the sale of timber would be split 50% each between Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine; if either party breached the contract, the other party had the right to terminate the contract, and the breaching party would bear liquidated damages amounting to 20% of the total funds of the other party. After the contract was signed, on March 19, 2004, Chaili Coal Mine delivered a RMB 10 million draft to Huadong Company, which was deposited into its general settlement account. Subsequently, Huadong Company misappropriated the RMB 10 million without authorization, constituting a fundamental breach of contract. Huaxia Bank's unauthorized consent to Huadong Company's use of the funds also constituted a breach of contract. Therefore, Chaili Coal Mine sought a judgment: (1) terminating the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber"; (2) ordering Huadong Company to return RMB 10 million in payment to Chaili Coal Mine; (3) ordering Huadong Company to bear liquidated damages of RMB 2 million; and (4) ordering Huaxia Bank to assume joint and several liability for the repayment of RMB 10 million. During the first-instance court debate, Chaili Coal Mine amended its claim, seeking to hold Huaxia Bank liable for supplementary compensation for RMB 7 million. Thereafter, Chaili Coal Mine further changed the scope of the funds for which it sought supplementary compensation from Huaxia Bank from RMB 7 million to RMB 10 million.  

Huadong Company argued: It agreed to terminate the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" but could not accept the RMB 2 million liquidated damages claimed by Chaili Coal Mine. Huadong Company had not received any capital contribution from Chaili Coal Mine; it had only received RMB 10 million remitted by a third party, Li Hongliang, and the legal consequences between itself and Li Hongliang bore no legal relationship to the original parties.  

Huaxia Bank argued: The claims of Chaili Coal Mine were unfounded. Huaxia Bank was only obligated to fulfill the matters promised in the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber," but those matters did not occur due to reasons attributable to Chaili Coal Mine itself. Chaili Coal Mine's claims against Huaxia Bank lacked both factual and legal basis and should be dismissed.  

The Tengzhou City People's Court of Shandong Province found the following facts at first instance: On March 16, 2004, Huadong Company, Chaili Coal Mine, and Huaxia Bank entered into a tripartite "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber," which mainly stipulated: Chaili Coal Mine and Huadong Company would jointly operate Indonesian timber; Huadong Company would bear the risks of import from abroad, while domestic sales risks would be shared by Chaili Coal Mine and Huadong Company; Chaili Coal Mine was responsible for providing RMB 10 million in funds, which were to be remitted to Huaxia Bank by March 18, 2004, as requested by Huadong Company, and Huadong Company would handle the application for issuance of letters of credit for international trade. When handling the application for issuance of letters of credit for international trade, a written consent opinion from Wen Zhongcheng, the responsible person of Chaili Coal Mine, was required, and Huaxia Bank, upon seeing Wen Zhongcheng's written consent opinion, would handle the issuance of letters of credit in accordance with the terms jointly applied for by Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine; after the timber arrived at port, Huaxia Bank would make payment in accordance with the relevant letter of credit terms, and the sales proceeds of the timber would be remitted to a new joint account opened by Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine at Huaxia Bank, under the supervision of Huaxia Bank; the transaction cycle for operating funds was 90 days; the profits from the sale of timber would be split 50% each between Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine, and Huadong Company would, within 7 days after the completion of timber sales, return the RMB 10 million in funds to Chaili Coal Mine along with the profit share due; if either party breached the contract, the other party had the right to terminate the contract, and the breaching party would bear liquidated damages amounting to 20% of the total funds of the other party, etc.  

After the contract was signed, on March 18, 2004, Chaili Coal Mine sent its employee Li Hongliang to deliver two bank drafts (payor: Li Hongliang; payee: Huadong Company) totaling RMB 10 million to Huadong Company. On March 19, Huadong Company issued a receipt to Chaili Coal Mine, stating: "Received from Chaili Coal Mine (Li Hongliang) investment funds, totaling RMB 10 million." On the same day, Huadong Company cashed the two drafts for RMB 10 million and deposited the funds into a general settlement account opened with Huaxia Bank on January 16, 2004. Thereafter, from March 22, 2004, Huadong Company began to withdraw funds from this general settlement account, and by September 21, 2004, the account balance was RMB 709,050.  

On September 22, 2004, Chaili Coal Mine sent a letter to Huaxia Bank, stating: "On March 16, 2004, through friendly consultations among your bank, Huadong Company, and Chaili Coal Mine, the 'Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber' was successfully signed. In accordance with Article 8 of the cooperation agreement, the transaction cycle for the cooperative operating funds has long expired. With respect to the letter of credit issuance terms originally provided by us, except for the clause requiring the signature of Mr. Wen Zhongcheng before funds are used, the other terms shall automatically lapse. Regarding the use and disposition of the remaining RMB 7 million in funds beyond the initial RMB 3 million paid out, we earnestly request strict compliance with the cooperation agreement, i.e., before the use and disposition of funds, a written consent opinion from our responsible person, Mr. Wang Yuhai or Mr. Wen Zhongcheng, is required." On the same day, Chen Gang, then a relationship manager of Huaxia Bank, signed a comment on the letter: "Please have both parties implement in accordance with the joint venture agreement signed on March 16, 2004." On January 27, 2005, Chen Gang sent a letter to Wang Yuhai, the mine director of Chaili Coal Mine, stating: With regard to the joint venture agreement, once the timber arrives at port, I will promptly inform you of the port of arrival and the time. Subsequently, Huadong Company never proceeded with the import of timber and continued to use checks to transfer funds to itself within the same city. By March 17, 2005, the balance in the aforementioned general settlement account was RMB 227.70, and no further transactions occurred thereafter.  

The Tengzhou City People's Court held at first instance: The "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" entered into by Chaili Coal Mine, Huadong Company, and Huaxia Bank did not violate the mandatory provisions of Chinese laws and administrative regulations and should be valid. The receipt issued by Huadong Company to Chaili Coal Mine recorded the receipt of RMB 10 million in investment funds, which was sufficient to establish that Chaili Coal Mine had fulfilled its capital contribution obligation under the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber." After receiving Chaili Coal Mine's funds, Huadong Company failed to use the funds in accordance with the contract and did not perform the obligation to import timber, constituting a fundamental breach of contract. The claim by Chaili Coal Mine for termination of the contract, return of the capital contribution, and assumption of liability for breach of contract was legally justified and supported. The "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" stipulated that when Huadong Company used the RMB 10 million funds from Chaili Coal Mine as security to handle an application for issuance of letters of credit for international trade, Huaxia Bank was required to review whether there was a written opinion from Wen Zhongcheng, the responsible person of Chaili Coal Mine. Therefore, Huaxia Bank played a role in supervising the use of funds in the joint operation of Indonesian timber between Chaili Coal Mine and Huadong Company. Huaxia Bank was not a party to the joint venture contract, and Chaili Coal Mine's capital contribution was not to be remitted directly to Huaxia Bank; it could only be deposited with Huaxia Bank by Chaili Coal Mine or Huadong Company. The declaration letter sent by Chaili Coal Mine to Huaxia Bank and the letter from Chen Gang indicated that Huaxia Bank was aware that the RMB 10 million capital contribution from Chaili Coal Mine had been received. When Huadong Company used the funds, Huaxia Bank knew and should have known that Huadong Company was using the guarantee funds provided by Chaili Coal Mine for the purpose of issuing letters of credit, yet it did not prevent Huadong Company from unilaterally using the funds, thereby frustrating the cooperative purpose sought by Chaili Coal Mine. Huaxia Bank's failure to fulfill its supervision and review obligations constituted a breach of commitment to Chaili Coal Mine and should bear supplementary compensation liability to Chaili Coal Mine. On November 21, 2005, the court rendered the civil judgment (2005) Teng Min Chu Zi No. 2716, ordering: (1) Termination of the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber"; (2) Huadong Company to return the joint venture capital contribution of RMB 10 million to Chaili Coal Mine; (3) Huadong Company to pay the agreed liquidated damages of RMB 2 million to Chaili Coal Mine; (4) Huaxia Bank to bear liability for compensation in the event of failure of Huadong Company to return the joint venture capital contribution of RMB 10 million to Chaili Coal Mine. Court acceptance fee of RMB 70,010 and other litigation costs of RMB 69,000 were to be borne by Huadong Company.  

Both Huadong Company and Huaxia Bank, dissatisfied with the first-instance judgment, appealed to the Zaozhuang Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province.  

Huadong Company appealed, arguing: (1) The facts found in the original judgment were erroneous. During the course of the cooperation, due to Chaili Coal Mine's breach of contract, the agreement could not continue to be performed, and Chaili Coal Mine should bear liability for compensation. (2) The application of law in the original judgment was erroneous. The liquidated damages of 20% of the contract amount confirmed in the original judgment far exceeded the losses and were manifestly unfair.  

Huaxia Bank appealed, arguing: (1) Procedural errors existed in the first instance. Chaili Coal Mine amended its claims during the first-instance trial, seeking supplementary compensation from Huaxia Bank for RMB 7 million, but the original judgment ordered Huaxia Bank to bear liability for RMB 10 million, which violated the law. (2) The facts found in the original judgment were erroneous. According to the "Supplementary Agreement," the joint venture agreement should be deemed invalid; the matters promised by Huaxia Bank in the tripartite agreement did not occur, and Huaxia Bank did not breach the contract. The original judgment's finding that the bank was aware that Chaili Coal Mine's RMB 10 million capital contribution had been received was erroneous. Chaili Coal Mine's failure to recover its funds was related to its own illegal or irregular operations and it should bear its own responsibility. Therefore, the appellate court was requested to revise the judgment and dismiss Chaili Coal Mine's claims against Huaxia Bank.  

Chaili Coal Mine argued in response: (1) Although it paid the funds one day late, Huadong Company raised no objection and accepted the payment, which should be deemed as Huadong Company's acknowledgment. Huadong Company had caused substantial losses to Chaili Coal Mine and should bear liability for breach of contract. (2) The agent had indeed expressed an intention in the first instance to relieve Huaxia Bank of liability for RMB 3 million, but Huaxia Bank denied that statement; according to the Rules of Evidence, that statement could not be used as evidence. The Supplementary Agreement did not have the effect of terminating the joint venture agreement. Huaxia Bank was fully aware of the source, specific purpose, and specific procedures for the use of the RMB 10 million funds but failed to supervise; it should bear liability for breach of contract. Li Hongliang's payment on behalf of Chaili Coal Mine was an act performed in the course of employment, which Huaxia Bank knew, and such conduct did not cause the losses.  

The Zaozhuang Intermediate People's Court confirmed the facts found by the first-instance court. It additionally found: On April 16, 2004, Chen Gang sent two text messages to Zhang Huaifu of Chaili Coal Mine, indicating that the timber imported from Indonesia would soon be shipped, etc.  

The intermediate court held in the second instance: The "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" signed by Huadong Company, Huaxia Bank, and Chaili Coal Mine should be confirmed as valid. The "Supplementary Agreement" signed by Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine, without the consent of Huaxia Bank, did not have the effect of terminating the "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber." The "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" was the only effective document governing the rights and obligations of all parties in this case. After receiving Chaili Coal Mine's funds, Huadong Company failed to use the funds in accordance with the contract, constituting a fundamental breach of contract and should bear liability for breach of contract. The "Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber" stipulated that Huaxia Bank was required to review whether there was a written consent opinion from Wen Zhongcheng, the responsible person of Chaili Coal Mine, when Huadong Company handled the application for issuance of letters of credit for international trade. Therefore, Huaxia Bank bore the responsibility of supervising the use of the RMB 10 million funds provided by Chaili Coal Mine in the joint operation of timber between Chaili Coal Mine and Huadong Company. Chen Gang, an employee of Huaxia Bank, directly participated in the contract negotiations, signing, and actual performance, sent text messages to conceal the fact that funds had been used, and also signed comments on the declaration letter submitted by Chaili Coal Mine to Huaxia Bank. These acts demonstrated that Huaxia Bank and its employees acting in the course of employment were fully aware of the source and specific procedures for the use of the RMB 10 million funds and bore the responsibility to remind Huadong Company to use the funds in accordance with the contract. Huaxia Bank not only failed to disclose the truth to Chaili Coal Mine but also, when Huadong Company used the funds, adopted means of fabricating facts and concealing the true situation, failing to fulfill its supervisory obligations, and should bear liability. The intermediate court accordingly dismissed the appeals and affirmed the original judgment, with appellate court acceptance fees of RMB 70,010 to be borne equally by Huaxia Bank and Huadong Company, each paying RMB 35,005.  

Huaxia Bank, dissatisfied with the second-instance judgment of the Zaozhuang Intermediate People's Court, applied for retrial with the Shandong High People's Court on September 12, 2006. On June 11, 2008, the Shandong High People's Court rendered the civil ruling (2007) Lu Min Jian Zi No. 123, ordering a retrial of this case.  

The Shandong High People's Court confirmed the facts previously found. It additionally found: From March 22, 2004, Huadong Company made deposits of RMB 2.3 million, RMB 7.7 million, and RMB 5 million, totaling RMB 15 million, into its general settlement account at Huaxia Bank Zhongshan Road Sub-branch. From March 22, 2004, to November 29, 2004, funds were withdrawn from this account successively. Among these, on April 21, 2004, RMB 3.5 million was withdrawn by check; on April 23, 2004, RMB 3 million was withdrawn by check; the payee in both cases was Huadong Company. The purpose of funds column on the transfer vouchers for these two sums was marked "Timber L/C". After March 17, 2005, no further transactions occurred in this account. The current account balance is RMB 227.60. The matters agreed upon regarding the import of timber and the application for issuance of letters of credit did not actually occur. During the first-instance trial, Chaili Coal Mine stated in court that the RMB 3 million of the RMB 10 million used by Huadong Company on April 23, 2004, had been authorized by Wen Zhongcheng, the responsible person of the mine, and requested that Huaxia Bank be ordered to bear supplementary compensation for RMB 7 million, but Huaxia Bank denied receiving any authorization. In the second instance, Chaili Coal Mine denied the statement it had made in the first instance.

The Shandong High People's Court held on retrial: The focus of the dispute in this case is whether Huaxia Bank should bear supplementary liability for the return of the RMB 10 million joint venture capital contribution by Huadong Company.

(1) Regarding the rights and obligations of the parties. According to the terms of the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber, Huaxia Bank's obligation was limited to, when Chaili Coal Mine directly remitted RMB 10 million into Huaxia Bank for Huadong Company to apply for a letter of credit, being responsible for verifying whether there was written consent from Chaili Coal Mine, then issuing the letter of credit, and supervising the recovered proceeds from future sales. In actual performance, Chaili Coal Mine did not remit the RMB 10 million letter of credit margin directly into Huaxia Bank as agreed, but instead delivered the bank draft directly to Huadong Company. After receiving the draft, Huadong Company deposited the draft amount into its general settlement account opened at Huaxia Bank, but did not clearly inform Huaxia Bank of the nature of the funds. Therefore, Huaxia Bank was unable to fulfill its supervisory obligation over these funds. The reason why the RMB 10 million of Chaili Coal Mine could not be recovered in this case was, first, that Chaili Coal Mine did not remit the funds into Huaxia Bank as agreed in the agreement, and the funds did not enter the letter of credit margin account; second, that Huadong Company, in violation of the contract, misappropriated the funds. In summary, the conditions for Huaxia Bank to perform its supervisory obligation were not fulfilled.

(2) Regarding whether Huaxia Bank knew the margin nature of the funds. To prove that Huaxia Bank knew the nature of the funds, Chaili Coal Mine provided corresponding evidence: first, two letters and a text message from Chen Gang to Chaili Coal Mine; second, the statements of Chaili Coal Mine's staff; third, the fund transfer vouchers noting "for timber letter of credit" as the purpose. First, the content reflected in the two letters from Chen Gang to Chaili Coal Mine had no direct connection to the disputed funds. Although the content of the text message forwarded by Chen Gang involved the timber matter, the evidence was insufficient to prove that Huaxia Bank knew the funds were of a margin nature. Second, the statements of Chaili Coal Mine's staff indicated that when the bank draft was handed over to Huadong Company, Chen Gang was present and went to the bank together to make the deposit. However, this evidence should be regarded in form as a statement of a party, with weak probative force, and Chen Gang denied it. Therefore, it cannot be determined that Chen Gang participated in the deposit process. Additionally, although the two outgoing checks bore the words "for timber letter of credit," because the funds were in Huadong Company's general settlement account, not in a margin account, it cannot be determined that Huaxia Bank knew the funds were margin funds yet failed to supervise. In summary, this evidence is insufficient to prove that Chen Gang actually participated in the deposit of the funds and knew they were letter of credit margin, nor to prove that Huaxia Bank knew the nature of the funds but failed to fulfill its supervisory obligation.

On July 13, 2008, the Shandong High People's Court, after discussion by the Court's Adjudication Committee, rendered Civil Judgment (2007) Lu Min Zai Zi No. 123, holding: (1) Revoke Civil Judgment (2006) Zao Min Si Zhong Zi No. 105 of the Zaozhuang Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province; (2) Affirm items one, two, and three of Civil Judgment (2005) Teng Min Chu Zi No. 2716 of the Tengzhou People's Court of Shandong Province; (3) Amend item four of Civil Judgment (2005) Teng Min Chu Zi No. 2716 of the Tengzhou People's Court of Shandong Province to: Dismiss Chaili Coal Mine's claim against Huaxia Bank.

Chaili Coal Mine, dissatisfied with Civil Judgment (2007) Lu Min Zai Zi No. 123 of the Shandong High People's Court, applied to this Court for retrial, alleging: (1) Huaxia Bank had a supervisory obligation over the use of Chaili Coal Mine's RMB 10 million funds. According to the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber, Chaili Coal Mine was to provide joint venture capital of RMB 10 million, to be deposited into Huadong Company's fund account at Huaxia Bank, to be used as guarantee funds when applying for a letter of credit. Once the funds were remitted into Huaxia Bank as special funds, Huaxia Bank was not permitted to allow Huadong Company to use or withdraw them at will. Therefore, Huaxia Bank had an inescapable supervisory responsibility over the use of the RMB 10 million, and not only when Huadong Company applied for a letter of credit, with no responsibility at other times. Otherwise, it would be inconsistent with the purpose of the special agreement for dedicated use. (2) The conditions for Huaxia Bank to supervise the use of the RMB 10 million funds in this case had been fulfilled. The RMB 10 million funds provided by Chaili Coal Mine were already in place, and Huaxia Bank had no right to require Chaili Coal Mine to remit the RMB 10 million directly to Huaxia Bank. Before the letter of credit was issued, the RMB 10 million did not yet have the nature of letter of credit margin. Huaxia Bank's claim that it could not fulfill its supervisory obligation because the funds were not deposited into a special account lacked factual and legal basis. As a professional financial service institution, if Huaxia Bank believed that the funds must be deposited into a special account, it should have explained and informed Chaili Coal Mine at the time of signing the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber, or at the latest, when the funds were deposited. Huadong Company would then naturally have been unable to misappropriate the funds. It was precisely because the RMB 10 million did not yet have the nature of letter of credit margin that the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber stipulated that Huaxia Bank had a supervisory obligation over the use of these funds. (3) Huaxia Bank was grossly negligent in failing to perform its supervisory obligation. First, Huaxia Bank knew of the deposit, withdrawal, and specific use of the RMB 10 million funds. Huaxia Bank's client manager, Chen Gang, participated throughout the negotiations for the tripartite joint operation of Indonesian timber and was fully aware that the specific use of the RMB 10 million funds was for timber letter of credit; the correspondence between Chen Gang and Chaili Coal Mine also indicated that he was clear and knew that the RMB 10 million funds were for dedicated use. In this situation, when Huadong Company misappropriated the funds, Huaxia Bank did not keep its promise and even maliciously concealed the fact that the funds in the account were misappropriated by Huadong Company, until the special funds for timber letter of credit in the account were completely depleted, causing irreparable substantial losses to Chaili Coal Mine. In summary, pursuant to Article 179, Paragraph 1, Subparagraphs (2) and (6) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, an application for retrial is filed.

Huaxia Bank responded in defense: Chaili Coal Mine's appeal contradicts the basic facts and involved numerous false statements during the court trial. Chaili Coal Mine's attempt throughout the previous trials to presume Huaxia Bank's obligations is legally unfounded. The determination of obligations must be based on law or agreement. The obligations of Huaxia Bank under the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber are clearly defined and the wording is clear. The "presumed" obligations unilaterally proposed by Chaili Coal Mine cannot be established. In this case, Huaxia Bank had no supervisory obligation over the RMB 10 million funds. The only supervisory obligation agreed upon by the three parties was to supervise the domestic sales proceeds of imported Indonesian timber (which must be deposited into a newly opened account). In fact, the Indonesian timber business did not occur at all, so there was no issue of Huaxia Bank performing a supervisory obligation. The facts (business) agreed upon in the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber did not occur, the precondition for Huaxia Bank to perform its obligation did not exist, and the objective conditions for supervision were not fulfilled. Therefore, Chaili Coal Mine's claim that Huaxia Bank should bear legal liability has no legal basis.

Huadong Company responded in defense: The Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber signed by Huadong Company, Chaili Coal Mine, and Huaxia Bank on March 16, 2004, did not represent the true intent of the parties. On the same day the agreement was signed, Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine also signed a Supplemental Agreement, confirming that the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber had no legal binding force. Later, Huaxia Bank also confirmed that the agreement was invalid. Based on the objective fact that Huadong Company and Chaili Coal Mine and Zaozhuang Mining (Group) Company had a cooperative development of Indonesian coal mines, the RMB 10 million paid by Chaili Coal Mine to Huadong Company could only be an upfront investment, not a "margin" for cooperative timber operation used for international trade letter of credit issuance. Therefore, neither Huadong Company nor Chaili Coal Mine performed the relevant procedures for international trade letter of credit issuance as agreed in the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber, and Huaxia Bank's supervisory obligation had no foundation. Thus, the original first instance, second instance, and retrial judgments finding the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber valid and that the RMB 10 million was a letter of credit margin were erroneous. Therefore, Huadong Company requests that the Supreme People's Court revoke Civil Judgment (2007) Lu Min Zai Zi No. 123 of the Shandong High People's Court, Civil Judgment (2006) Zao Min Si Zhong Zi No. 105 of the Zaozhuang Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province, and Civil Judgment (2005) Teng Min Chu Zi No. 2716 of the Tengzhou People's Court of Shandong Province, dismiss the lawsuit filed by the respondent on retrial, Chaili Coal Mine, and the litigation costs of the first and second instances shall be borne by Chaili Coal Mine.

This Court confirms the facts found in the original trial.

This Court holds on retrial: The focus of the dispute in this case is whether Huaxia Bank should bear supplementary liability for the loss of Chaili Coal Mine's RMB 10 million capital contribution.

The key to resolving this focus is to determine whether Huaxia Bank had a supervisory obligation over the RMB 10 million funds in this case. If it had a supervisory obligation and was able to supervise but failed to perform its duty, it should bear the legal consequences arising therefrom; if it had no such supervisory obligation, it should not bear liability.

A bank's supervisory obligation over depositors' funds mainly comes from two sources: first, the provisions of laws, regulations, and rules; second, special agreements between the depositor and the bank. The RMB 10 million at issue in this case was, in nature, the reserve fund for the letter of credit margin, deposited by Chaili Coal Mine through Huadong Company into Huadong Company's general settlement account. According to Article 30 of the Commercial Banking Law of the People's Republic of China and Article 11 of the Measures for the Administration of Bank Accounts of the People's Bank of China, the account holder has the autonomous right to dispose of funds in a general settlement account, and no unit, including the bank, may arbitrarily restrict, freeze, or deduct such funds; otherwise, it would constitute an infringement on the account holder. Therefore, Huaxia Bank had no statutory supervisory authority or obligation over the RMB 10 million at issue. Article 3 of the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber stipulates: "Party B (i.e., Chaili Coal Mine) is responsible for providing funds (RMB 10 million) for this cooperation. Before March 18, 2004, it shall remit the funds to Party C (i.e., Huaxia Bank) as required by Party A (i.e., Huadong Company), to be used by Party A for applying for an international trade letter of credit. However, when applying for the international trade letter of credit, the written consent opinion of Chaili Coal Mine's responsible person, Wen Zhongcheng, must be obtained. Party C, upon seeing the written consent opinion of Wen Zhongcheng, shall handle the letter of credit issuance matters in accordance with the terms applied for by Parties A and B." Based on this, it can be determined that when Huaxia Bank handled matters related to the issuance of a letter of credit for Huadong Company, it should verify whether there was a written consent opinion from Chaili Coal Mine's responsible person, Wen Zhongcheng. Only with Wen Zhongcheng's written consent could Huaxia Bank handle the relevant matters for Huadong Company for the issuance of the letter of credit, including the withdrawal of funds for the purpose of issuing the letter of credit. If, without Wen Zhongcheng's written consent, Huaxia Bank allowed Huadong Company to withdraw the funds for the purpose of issuing the letter of credit, it would have failed to perform its supervisory obligation under the agreement and should bear liability for breach of contract.

The above agreement did not clearly specify whether Huaxia Bank had a supervisory obligation when Huadong Company withdrew the funds for purposes other than applying for a letter of credit; this constitutes an unclear contract term. The parties dispute this unclear matter. Chaili Coal Mine argues that the purpose of signing the tripartite agreement was to ensure dedicated use of funds and the safety of the capital contribution. According to the purpose interpretation, it should be determined that Article 3 of the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber imposed on Huaxia Bank an inescapable supervisory responsibility and review obligation over the RMB 10 million funds, and that regardless of whether Huadong Company used the funds for a letter of credit, Huaxia Bank should be responsible for supervision. This Court holds that for contract terms that are unclear and disputed by the parties, various methods of interpretation, including purpose interpretation, can be used to comprehensively ascertain the true intent of the parties in concluding the contract. However, as for purpose interpretation, it should not be based solely on the contractual purpose that one party expects to achieve. Instead, it should be interpreted according to the common contractual purpose of the parties as understood by a reasonable third person who has no interest in the contract. Moreover, purpose interpretation should not lead to infringement of the legitimate rights and interests of others or conflict with laws and regulations. In this case, Chaili Coal Mine did have concerns about the safety of its capital contribution and specifically entered into contract terms with Huadong Company and Huaxia Bank for this purpose. However, given that the three parties had clearly agreed and arranged when and how the capital contribution of Chaili Coal Mine would be supervised, merely based on the effect intention and contractual purpose of one party, Chaili Coal Mine, to presume that the counterparties, Huaxia Bank and Huadong Company, must additionally undertake obligations beyond those agreed, is difficult to say it conforms to the common contractual purpose of the parties. From a practical analysis, the RMB 10 million was deposited in Huadong Company's general settlement account and commingled with other funds in the account. Huaxia Bank was in fact unable to distinguish it and implement comprehensive supervision separately. If, based on purpose interpretation, it is presumed that Huaxia Bank had such an obligation, it could only lead to Huaxia Bank restricting the use of all commingled funds in Huadong Company's general settlement account, which would undoubtedly infringe upon Huadong Company's autonomous right to dispose of the funds deposited in its general settlement account. This would be contrary to laws and regulations. Therefore, this Court holds that Huaxia Bank had no supervisory obligation over Huadong Company's withdrawal of the funds from its general settlement account for purposes other than issuing a letter of credit.

On September 22, 2004, Chaili Coal Mine sent a letter to Huaxia Bank, stating: regarding the RMB 10 million it provided, "except for the RMB 3 million paid in advance, the use and disposal of the remaining RMB 7 million funds sincerely require strict implementation of the cooperative agreement, i.e., the use and disposal of the funds must have the written consent opinion of our responsible person, Mr. Wang Yuhai or Mr. Wen Zhongcheng, before they can be carried out." This letter modified the letter of credit supervisory obligation of Huaxia Bank stipulated in the previous tripartite agreement and expanded the scope of fund supervision by Huaxia Bank, which in nature should be regarded as a new offer. In response, Chen Gang, then client manager of Huaxia Bank, endorsed on the letter: "The parties shall execute in accordance with the joint venture agreement signed on March 16, 2004." This in effect indicated that Huaxia Bank did not agree to the request of Chaili Coal Mine to modify the tripartite agreement. Moreover, this offer did not obtain the consent of Huadong Company. Therefore, Chaili Coal Mine's letter could not unilaterally change the terms of the tripartite agreement.

In summary, this Court holds that, according to the terms of Article 3 of the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber, Huaxia Bank had a supervisory obligation over Huadong Company's withdrawal of the RMB 10 million funds for the purpose of applying for a letter of credit. Apart from that, there were no other supervisory obligations.

Regarding the disbursement of the RMB 10 million by Huadong Company, for the disbursements of RMB 3.5 million and RMB 3 million on April 21 and April 23, 2004, respectively, the "purpose of funds" column on the transfer checks indicated "for timber letter of credit." Although Huadong Company did not actually use the above funds for timber letter of credit, when it withdrew the two sums in the name of applying for a letter of credit, the conditions for Huaxia Bank's supervision stipulated in Article 3 of the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber were already met. Huaxia Bank was obligated to verify whether this matter had obtained the written consent of Wen Zhongcheng. Chaili Coal Mine admitted in court that the RMB 3 million disbursed on April 23 for "timber letter of credit" had obtained the written consent of Wen Zhongcheng, but argued that it consented to Huadong Company's withdrawal of the funds for the purpose of applying for a letter of credit. However, Huadong Company did not actually apply for a letter of credit, so Huaxia Bank should still bear liability for this loss. But according to the Agreement on Cooperative Operation of Indonesian Timber, Huaxia Bank only had a formal review obligation regarding Huadong Company's use of the funds for applying for a letter of credit. That is, when Huadong Company withdrew the funds for the purpose of a letter of credit, as long as there was written consent from Wen Zhongcheng, the responsible person of Chaili Coal Mine, Huaxia Bank could release the funds. As for whether Huadong Company actually used the funds for a letter of credit after withdrawal, or how it used them, that was beyond Huaxia Bank's control. Therefore, the above argument of Chaili Coal Mine is untenable. Article 74 of the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings stipulates: "During the litigation process, the people's court shall confirm the facts unfavorable to the party and the evidence admitted by the party in the complaint, defense, statements, and the pleadings of the agent ad litem, unless the party repents and adduces sufficient evidence to the contrary to overturn them." Since Chaili Coal Mine failed to provide contrary evidence to overturn its admission that Huadong Company's withdrawal of RMB 3 million had its consent, this Court confirms this fact and accordingly exempts Huaxia Bank from supervisory liability for that RMB 3 million. However, Huaxia Bank, while the conditions for supervision were met and it was able to supervise, violated the tripartite agreement and negligently failed to perform its supervisory obligation, allowing Huadong Company to misappropriate RMB 3.5 million under the name of "timber letter of credit." This clearly constituted a breach of contract and Huaxia Bank should bear corresponding liability for breach.

In summary, this Court holds that Huaxia Bank should bear supervisory liability for the RMB 3.5 million misappropriated by Huadong Company under the name of "timber letter of credit." The original retrial judgment of the Shandong High People's Court, which found that Huaxia Bank was not liable, was erroneous and should be corrected. Pursuant to Article 186, Paragraph 1 and Article 153, Paragraph 1, Subparagraph (3) of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China, Article 94, Subparagraph (4), Article 107, and Article 114 of the Contract Law of the People's Republic of China, and Article 74 of the Supreme People's Court's Several Provisions on Evidence in Civil Proceedings, this Court renders judgment as follows:

1. Revoke Civil Judgment (2007) Lu Min Zai Zi No. 123 of the Shandong High People's Court and Civil Judgment (2006) Zao Min Si Zhong Zi No. 105 of the Zaozhuang Intermediate People's Court of Shandong Province;

2. Affirm items one, two, and three of Civil Judgment (2005) Teng Min Chu Zi No. 2716 of the Tengzhou People's Court of Shandong Province;

3. Amend item four of Civil Judgment (2005) Teng Min Chu Zi No. 2716 of the Tengzhou People's Court of Shandong Province to: Huaxia Bank Co., Ltd., Qingdao Branch shall bear liability for compensation within the scope of RMB 3.5 million for the failure of Qingdao Free Trade Zone Huadong International Trade Co., Ltd. to return the RMB 10 million joint venture capital contribution to the Chaili Coal Mine of Zaozhuang Mining (Group) Co., Ltd.

The above payment obligations shall be fulfilled within 15 days from the date of service of this judgment. In case of late payment, the payor shall pay double the interest on the amount due during the period of delay in performance in accordance with Article 229 of the Civil Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China.

First instance case acceptance fee of RMB 70,010 and other litigation fees of RMB 69,000 shall be borne by Huadong Company as per the first instance judgment; second instance case acceptance fee of RMB 70,010 shall be borne by Huadong Company in the amount of RMB 35,005, by Huaxia Bank in the amount of RMB 12,252, and by Chaili Coal Mine in the amount of RMB 22,753.

This judgment is final.
